title: New Directions in Cognitive-Environmental Research: Applications to Urban Planning and Design
research_question: To review the interdisciplinary cognitive-environmental literature to examine how and where this research takes on planning concerns, directly or indirectly, and what it might mean for future planning practice, research, and teaching.

findings.consequent: impact on academic research in social sciences
findings.mechanism: Lynch's concepts provided a framework for understanding urban experience.
findings.quote: Lynch acknowledges that his work may have had greater impact on academic research in the social sciences than in planning and design

findings.consequent: evolution outside urban design into human geography and environmental psychology
findings.mechanism: Influenced by Edward Tolman's seminal work.
findings.quote: Cognitive mapping research continued to evolve outside of urban design within human geography and environmental psychology

findings.consequent: development through successive stages of refinement (landmark, route, survey/map knowledge)
findings.mechanism: Theory of spatial learning.
findings.quote: cognitive maps may develop through successive stages of refinement, beginning with landmark know-ledge, then route knowledge, and finally survey/map knowledge

findings.consequent: spatial learning in urban environments
findings.mechanism: Human mobility plays a significant role in this literature.
findings.quote: Wayfinding traditionally has been the primary means of spatial learning in urban environments

findings.antecedent: Varying travel experiences (route or mode choice)
findings.consequent: different cognitive maps
findings.mechanism: Cognitive effort varies by travel mode.
findings.quote: Varying travel experiences, whether differentiated by route or mode choice, can result in different cognitive maps.

findings.consequent: quality of destination knowledge
findings.mechanism: Reduced cognitive engagement during passive travel.
findings.quote: destination knowledge is of poorer quality among passive travelers, such as car or transit passengers, compared with car drivers and walkers

findings.consequent: shaping of urban choices (where and whether to go)
findings.mechanism: Proliferation of mobile devices and applications.
findings.quote: Navigation technologies are part of a broader expansion in the use of information and communication technologies that shape our choices in the urban realm

findings.consequent: cognitive engagement in vehicular locomotion
findings.mechanism: Removes the burden of cognitive engagement.
findings.quote: Automation of personal vehicle travel, although still nascent, could also remove the burden of any cognitive engagement in vehicular locomotion

findings.consequent: user travel and outcomes (travel times)
findings.mechanism: NITs are understood as a means of enhancing user travel.
findings.quote: enhanced information from NITs is most often understood as a means of enhancing user travel, improving travel times and outcomes

findings.consequent: transit use
findings.quote: better transit information has been shown to have a significant positive relationship with transit use

findings.consequent: legibility for older adults
findings.mechanism: Designed for populations facing learning and directional challenges.
findings.quote: propose using landmarks in a navigation system to increase legibility for older adults

findings.antecedent: Spatial-behavioral products of NITs (tweets, smartcards, cell phone use)
findings.consequent: insights into mobility choices and behaviors
findings.mechanism: Generate insights into mobility choices and behaviors.
findings.quote: Researchers are also using the spatial-behavioral products of NITs such as tweets, smartcards, and cell phone use to generate insights into mobility choices and behaviors

findings.consequent: link between place-based experience and public health outcomes
findings.mechanism: Incorporates health metrics with precise environmental data.
findings.quote: Citizen sensing, which incorporates health metrics from wearable devices with precise environmental data, can link place-based experience with personal and public health outcomes

findings.consequent: encoding spatial information within the brain
findings.mechanism: Central to neurobiological conceptualization of cognitive mapping.
findings.quote: At the center of the neurobiological conceptualization of cognitive mapping is the hippocampus

findings.consequent: encoding of real-world places into the brain
findings.mechanism: Particular neurons fire when features of a specific place are sensed.
findings.quote: Real-world places are encoded into the brain with place cells, particular neurons that fire when features of a specific place are sensed.

findings.consequent: map-like arrangement within the brain (firing sequentially as animal moves)
findings.mechanism: Hexagonally arranged grid cells.
findings.quote: grid cells are arranged in a map-like way within the brain, with these neurons firing sequentially as an animal moves through space.

findings.consequent: enlargement of posterior hippocampi
findings.mechanism: Physiological observation of map-learning.
findings.quote: the effect of the map-learning and long-term navigational experience of London (UK) taxi drivers has been physiologically observed in the enlargement of their posterior hippocampi

findings.antecedent: Cognitive spatial mapping strategies (vs. memorized route instructions)
findings.consequent: hippocampal size
findings.mechanism: Different navigation strategies impact brain structure.
findings.quote: subjects using cognitive spatial mapping strategies to navigate had larger hippocampi compared with those responding to memorized route instructions

findings.consequent: hippocampal role in spatial learning and knowledge
findings.mechanism: Episodic memory likely evolved from spatial learning.
findings.quote: the human capacity for episodic memory in the hippocampus likely evolved from its early role in spatial learning and knowledge

findings.consequent: organization of life's experiences and support for planning goal-oriented behavior
findings.mechanism: Cognitive maps organize specific events in systematic fashion appropriate to the dimensions of the relevant context.
findings.quote: Tolman conceived of cognitive maps as extending generally to mapping life's experiences in any behaviorally relevant domain. He conceived the function of these maps as organizing specific events

findings.consequent: encoding of spatial, temporal, and situational context; systematic organization of information for goal-oriented behavior
findings.mechanism: Hippocampus encodes a wide variety of information about context and creates systematic organization.
findings.quote: Hippocampal function embodies each of these properties, showing that, in addition to spatial context, the hippocampus encodes a wide variety of information about temporal and situational context

findings.consequent: engagement of cognitive map (spatial or non-spatial)
findings.mechanism: Humans navigate whether moving through space or through a situated but nonspatial challenge.
findings.quote: The goals-oriented processes of the brain may engage the cognitive map whether spatial or not.

findings.consequent: wellbeing (emotional state, mental health)
findings.mechanism: Environmental qualities and psychological perceptions (prospect and refuge, sound, views, safety, vegetation, walkability) influence wellbeing.
findings.quote: Research in psychology has also increased our understanding of the role of place and place-based experience in wellbeing overall.

findings.consequent: health (biomarkers like cortisol, telomere length)
findings.mechanism: Significant interactions among urban environment, social disadvantage, and health.
findings.quote: Biomarkers, such as the stress hormone cortisol and chromosome telomere length, for example, can demonstrate significant interactions among urban environment, social disadvantage, and health

findings.consequent: mitigating risks for Alzheimer's disease
findings.quote: cognitive mapping and spatial thinking may be associated with other significant health-related factors, even potentially mitigating risks for Alzheimer's disease

findings.antecedent: Road network configuration (e.g., number of turns)
findings.consequent: route choices
findings.mechanism: Space syntax theory and methods.
findings.quote: the configuration of a road network, such the number of turns it requires of a traveler, can significantly shape route choices.

findings.consequent: understanding spatial determinants of health (e.g., physical activity)
findings.mechanism: Can be deployed more broadly to understand spatial determinants of health.
findings.quote: Space syntax can be deployed more broadly to understand the spatial determinants of health, such as physical activity

findings.consequent: scene-recognition memory
findings.mechanism: Studies comparing computer navigation with paper maps.
findings.quote: poorer scene-recognition memory for those using routing aids

findings.consequent: map and route knowledge
findings.mechanism: Studies comparing computer navigation with paper maps.
findings.quote: superior map and route knowledge for paper map users

findings.consequent: travel times, direction errors, sketch maps
findings.mechanism: Studies comparing computer navigation with paper maps.
findings.quote: slower travel times, more direction errors, and poorer sketch maps for GPS users

findings.consequent: quality of sketch maps (London)
findings.mechanism: Compared with subjects reporting no or minimal GPS use.
findings.quote: Regular GPS users draw poorer, less complete sketch maps of London compared with subjects reporting no or minimal GPS use

findings.antecedent: Individuals' power and control over proximate conditions
findings.consequent: goal-oriented behaviors enabled by cognitive mapping
findings.mechanism: Perceptions of personal power directly affect cognitive processes.
findings.quote: the goal-oriented behaviors enabled by cognitive mapping are significantly modified by individuals' power and control over proximate conditions

findings.consequent: effort and performance
findings.quote: perceived control increasing effort and performance

findings.consequent: broader social objectives in a complex, diverse city
findings.mechanism: Hippocampus facilitates goals-oriented behavior, and active spatial learning contributes to its development.
findings.quote: healthy brain functioning, specifically the hippocampus, may complement broader social objectives in a complex, diverse city.

findings.consequent: hippocampal development
findings.quote: engaging in active spatial learning contributes to its development

findings.consequent: personal wellbeing
findings.mechanism: Lack of power may alienate individuals.
findings.quote: People value control over their environments, and lack of power may alienate individuals from their surroundings.

findings.antecedent: Active, choice-laden environments stimulating goals-oriented behaviors
findings.consequent: development of hippocampus and long-term health
findings.quote: Active, choice-laden environments for stimulating goals-oriented behaviors may stimulate the development of the hippocampus and long-term health.

findings.consequent: measurement of brain responses to environments and activities (e.g., alpha waves for relaxation)
findings.mechanism: Directly measure previously inaccessible features of mental maps.
findings.quote: Tools such as mobile electroencephalograms (EEGs) directly measure how the brain responds to environments and activities

findings.antecedent: Planners and designers affording control and agency (individual and community levels)
findings.consequent: human sense of control and agency within environments
findings.mechanism: Humans seek a sense of control and agency.
findings.quote: Planners and designers can and should afford that control at the levels of both the individual and community

findings.antecedent: Community-based design and decision making allowing for reconfiguration of urban places
findings.consequent: positive engagement in the urban realm and urban imageability
findings.mechanism: Opening streets and public spaces to more continuous change, if imbued with a sense of personal control over change, may increase imageability.
findings.quote: community-based design and decision making that allows for reconfiguration can stimulate positive engagement in the urban realm.

findings.consequent: specific types of spatial learning that stimulate hippocampus development
findings.mechanism: Our review highlights the fact that NITs diminish specific types of spatial learning.
findings.quote: Our review highlights the fact that NITs diminish specific types of spatial learning that stimulate the development of the hippocampus.

findings.antecedent: Smart city aspects (driverless vehicles, augmented reality)
findings.consequent: residents' knowledge of or sense of control over surroundings
findings.quote: Aspects of smart cities such as driverless vehicles and augmented reality on the street may decrease residents' knowledge of or sense of control over their surroundings.

findings.consequent: reinforcement of spatiality of daily life
findings.mechanism: Planners can work with educators to develop physical, technological, and social approaches to making the city legible.
findings.quote: Interventions, for example, may include unmappable spaces where certain types of navigation or other technologies are deactivated by default.

findings.antecedent: User-generated experiential, cognitive, and affective data
findings.consequent: incorporation into urban information systems for planning
findings.mechanism: Provides multiple opportunities to link applied social science research to mapping technologies and urban representation.
findings.quote: Urban information systems can incorporate user-generated experiential, cognitive, and affective data from city residents into planning research

findings.consequent: individuals making economic choices across urban landscape
findings.mechanism: Most used urban information systems.
findings.quote: the most used urban information systems are geosocial media like Google Search or Yelp that help individuals make economic choices across the urban landscape.

findings.antecedent: Planners and designers increasing legibility of noncommercial aspects of the city (e.g., affective states, sociopolitical variability)
findings.consequent: urban information systems' utility
findings.mechanism: Revealing invisible aspects of urban fabric.
findings.quote: Planners and designers can increase the legibility of noncommercial aspects of the city, revealing, for example, affective states, such as via emotion mapping, or sociopolitical variability

findings.consequent: multiple images experienced differently by different users; opportunities for city to speak to people, users to author experiences, civic education
findings.mechanism: Presents new opportunities for the city to speak to people.
findings.quote: digital devices and applications present new opportunities for the city to speak to people, for users to author and disseminate their own experiences and perspectives on the urban environment, and for civic education.

findings.antecedent: Waze app routing drivers through residential streets
findings.consequent: conflicts over expectations, self-image, and sense of control
findings.mechanism: Highlights changes caused by smart technologies.
findings.quote: The situation highlights the changes to expectations, self-image and city image, and sense of control that smart technologies are causing.

findings.consequent: modification of environmental effects (e.g., restorative effects of nature)
findings.mechanism: Environmental effects are likely modified significantly by sociocultural factors.
findings.quote: environmental effects are likely modified significantly by sociocultural factors

findings.consequent: salience of space to human experience overall
findings.mechanism: Whether understood in the context of Lynch or neurobiological models of spatial learning and behavior.
findings.quote: Technological urban futures may diminish the salience of space to human experience overall

findings.consequent: opportunities for individuals and communities to engage in image formation
findings.quote: More flexible, configurable streets and spaces may provide opportunities for individuals and communities to more deeply engage in image formation.

findings.consequent: urban spatial experiences understood as stories we tell ourselves
findings.mechanism: Reinforces that urban spatial experiences can be understood as stories we tell ourselves.
findings.quote: An enhanced understanding of how the brain works, specifically the spatial-episodic nature of memory in the hippocampus, also reinforces that urban spatial experiences can be understood as stories we tell ourselves.

findings.antecedent: City design allowing urban dwellers to devise and achieve their own objectives
findings.consequent: salience of urban experience (physical or hybrid virtual-physical space)
findings.quote: City design that allows urban dwellers to devise and achieve their own objectives is likely to be more salient

findings.antecedent: Data and health scientists claiming cities as quantifiable terrain for smart interventions
findings.consequent: need for planners and designers to assert priorities (humane technological future)
findings.mechanism: Planners and designers possess abiding values and concerns.
findings.quote: Planners and designers, however, possess abiding values and concerns that may not be thoughtfully addressed without their participation in—even if to oppose the formulation of data-driven, behavior-aware urbanization.

findings.antecedent: Neuroscientific findings relevant to human experience of urban life
findings.consequent: new planners' ability to assert priorities among urban science arrivistes
findings.mechanism: Teaching neuroscientific findings can provide new planners with an enhanced ability.
findings.quote: Teaching not just quantitative urban science but also neuroscientific findings relevant to the human experience of urban life can provide new planners with an enhanced ability to assert our priorities among urban science arrivistes.

findings.antecedent: Lynch's emphasis on imageability related to sense of capability and control
findings.consequent: importance for planning and design education
findings.quote: Lynch, too, should remain an important part of planning and design education, but with a refocused emphasis on the idea that imageability is closely related to a sense of capability and control of our environment.

findings.consequent: wellbeing dependent on control of one's narrative and environment
findings.mechanism: In cities that are increasingly passivizing due to new technology and limits on participation.
findings.quote: planners should recognize that humans are inherently spatial actors whose wellbeing depends in part on control of one's own narrative and environment.

mechanisms: Cognitive maps organize specific events in systematic fashion appropriate to the dimensions of the relevant context, supporting expectancies and planning of behavior to obtain sought goals.
Hippocampal function embodies properties of spatial, temporal, and situational context, creating a systematic organization of information for goal-oriented behavior.
Humans seek a sense of control and agency within their environments, and lack of power may alienate individuals.
Active spatial learning contributes to hippocampal development.
Mobile EEGs directly measure brain responses to environments and activities, helping determine best practices.
Community-based design and decision making that allows for reconfiguration can stimulate positive engagement and increase urban imageability if imbued with personal control.
NITs diminish specific types of spatial learning that stimulate hippocampus development.
Space syntax can be deployed to understand spatial determinants of health.
Environmental qualities and psychological perceptions (prospect and refuge, sound, views, safety, vegetation, walkability) influence wellbeing.
implementation_implications: Planners and designers should promote public spaces, transportation systems, and development patterns that provide cognitively engaging choices to residents across the life span and socioeconomic spectrum.
Increased understanding of diverse cognitive types is crucial, especially for groups with diminished navigation abilities (e.g., elderly).
Planners and designers should afford control and agency at individual and community levels.
Planners and designers can encourage innately reconfigurable urban places to stimulate positive engagement and imageability.
Planners should work with educators to develop physical, technological, and social approaches to making the city legible, even as it continues its long-term technological transformation.
Interventions may include unmappable spaces where certain types of navigation or other technologies are deactivated by default.
Urban information systems can incorporate user-generated experiential, cognitive, and affective data from city residents into planning research, community engagement processes, and praxis.
Planners and designers can increase the legibility of noncommercial aspects of the city (e.g., affective states, sociopolitical variability).
Urban planners must consider their regulatory role regarding NITs (e.g., Waze app conflicts).
Best practices for managing NITs in local communities should account for discontinuities between perceptions and expectations of travelers and locals.
Cognitive-environmental findings can provide guidance for urban design, promoting flexible, configurable streets and spaces for image formation.
City design that allows urban dwellers to devise and achieve their own objectives is likely to be more salient.

Planning scholars and educators should present Lynch and cognitive-environmental research in tandem, emphasizing cognitively engaged practices in environmental health, transportation, and urban design.
Planners and designers should use neuroscientific findings to assert priorities among urban science arrivistes, focusing on humane technological futures.
Lynch's emphasis on imageability related to a sense of capability and control should remain important for education.

tables.description: Citations of The Image of the City across disciplines (1960-2017)

limitations: The review acknowledges that findings from neurobiology and cognitive psychology are typically made in an individualized, humanistic context, though psychologists also examine sociocultural concerns.
The authors note that the literatures overall, though disparate, present a nuanced picture.
The authors state that cognitive-environmental research does not provide specific formal guidance given caveats about sociocultural factors and differing cognitive capabilities.
The authors acknowledge that the effects of NITs on the accuracy or detail of one's cognitive map and whether it affects travel behavior and access remain understudied despite their proliferation.
